definition: The Lai–Robbins lower bound gives an asymptotic lower bound on the regret that any uniformly good algorithm must incur in the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem.
details: The original result was proved by Tze Leung Lai and Herbert Robbins in 1985 for parametric exponential families. Later work extended the statement to more general classes of distributions.

explainer.lead: The Lai–Robbins lower bound sets an asymptotic floor on the regret any uniformly good algorithm must incur in stochastic multi-armed bandits. It matters because it tells you when a bandit algorithm is essentially as good as possible.

tiers.eli5: It is a speed limit for guessing games: no matter how clever your strategy, you cannot lose less than a certain amount over time.
tiers.practitioner: Bandit engineers compare an algorithm's regret curve against this bound to judge optimality. A pitfall is applying it outside its assumptions, since the original proof covers parametric exponential families.
tiers.paperLevel: Gives an asymptotic lower bound on regret for uniformly good algorithms in stochastic multi-armed bandits. Proved by Lai and Robbins in 1985 for parametric exponential families, later extended to more general distribution classes.

explainer.example: An engineer plots a bandit algorithm's regret over many rounds and finds it approaches the Lai–Robbins floor, indicating near-optimal exploration.
